synthesis: This lecture joins three levels of synaptic plasticity: experimental phenomena (LTP/LTD/STDP), proposed molecular mechanisms (NMDA-dependent \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) signaling and AMPA trafficking), and abstract learning rules. A basic Hebbian rule amplifies high-variance eigenmodes of input covariance but also creates positive feedback and unbounded growth. Synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM stabilize the system through global normalization, local weight-dependent decay, and a dynamic threshold, respectively.
commonTraps: Equating LTP/LTD with one \(NMDA/\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) pathway even though mechanisms vary across synapses and contexts.
Using only coincident high activity in basic Hebbian learning and overlooking centered covariance and depression.
Treating an eigenvector as a particular neuron.
Claiming that covariance “must be positive” without writing a quadratic-form proof of PSD.
Confusing directional selection with stabilization of the norm.
Equating Hebbian learning with PCA without stating its assumptions.
Assuming dopamine is the third factor in every form of reward learning.
The Hebbian-learning/PCA relationship holds only under particular linear, statistical, and stabilizing assumptions; “Hebbian = PCA” is not a universal identity.

synthesis: A machine-learning problem must specify its representation or architecture, objective or loss, and optimization or learning rule. Linear regression is the transparent example: the squared-error gradient decomposes into a data-dependent Hebbian-like term and a weight-dependent stabilizing term and admits a normal-equation closed form. In a deep network, backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule, carrying output error through transposed weights and local activation derivatives to each layer.
commonTraps: Conflating architecture, loss, and optimizer.
Forgetting that the gradient points uphill and the update needs a negative sign.
Omitting matrix shapes and therefore misplacing transposes in matrix calculus.
Attempting a direct inverse for a singular design matrix.
Assuming optimization of a deep linear network is itself linear or convex.
Treating backpropagation as an established biological synaptic mechanism.
Reading an informal historical aside as a rigorous technical conclusion.

Do not describe backpropagation as a biological mechanism in which error is directly sent back to neurons. Label it as a training algorithm and distinguish its formal resemblance to three-factor plasticity from its mechanistic differences.

synthesis: The visual hierarchy is not merely an anatomical list but a computational organization in which receptive-field size, feature complexity, history dependence, and invariance change by stage. LNP first projects a stimulus onto a linear receptive field, maps the drive through a nonlinearity to a rate, and uses a Poisson process to describe spikes. DoG, Gabor, and nonseparable spatiotemporal kernels summarize center-surround, orientation, and motion selectivity.
commonTraps: Treating a receptive field only as a geometric region in visual space.
Using raw luminance and contrast interchangeably.
Leaving the sign or flip convention of a convolution kernel unstated.
Assuming a feature map is a copy of the original image rather than a map of filter responses.
Confusing Gabor orientation, phase, and spatial frequency.
Assuming a separable spatiotemporal receptive field is automatically direction-selective.
Equating an anatomical hierarchy with one purely feedforward computation.

Do not describe a receptive field only as a screen “location”; it is a stimulus-response relationship. Distinguish a linear receptive field, classical receptive field, and experimental definition. Sparse-noise receptive-field mapping provides a useful transfer example.

synthesis: STA is both a descriptive average and, under a linear model, Gaussian white stimulation, and a suitable nonlinearity, a filter estimator. Matrix least squares reveals why: white stimulation makes the design covariance approximately a scalar identity, reducing the normal equation to a stimulus-response correlation. Recovering the nonlinearity yields an LNP model that can predict new stimuli, but multiple relevant dimensions, even-symmetric nonlinearities, or correlated stimulation can make the STA zero or biased.
commonTraps: Treating the STA only as an image average without specifying time-lag alignment.
Leaving matrix orientation unstated and confusing \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) with KS.
Omitting the large-sample and equal-variance assumptions behind white covariance.
Equating STA amplitude unconditionally with physical filter gain.
Concluding from \(STA=0\) that a neuron has no receptive field.
Forgetting to divide by bin width when recovering F.
Evaluating a model on its training fit instead of held-out prediction.
Distinguish the STA as a descriptive average, linear-filter estimator, and LNP-model component. They are related under particular assumptions, not unconditionally equivalent.

synthesis: Barlow's efficient coding is a normative hypothesis: under resource and noise constraints, a sensory system should reduce predictable redundancy while retaining useful information. Information theory quantifies predictability and transmission through surprise, entropy, and mutual information. Atick and Redlich model the retina as a noisy linear encoder and decoder that lowers redundancy under fixed-information and output-capacity constraints. Decorrelation is nonunique; rotational symmetry together with locality and related constraints can select a center-surround form.
commonTraps: Treating efficient coding as a uniquely established mechanism rather than a normative hypothesis.
Equating entropy unconditionally with useful information.
Calling a negative differential entropy an error.
Assuming \(MI=0\) means only zero linear correlation; when well-defined, it means independence.
Optimizing only decorrelation while ignoring noise and output capacity.
Assuming that the whitening solution is unique.
Presenting the normative center-surround prediction as singular causal evidence.
Distinguish entropy, differential entropy, mutual information, redundancy, and channel capacity. Avoid unconditional claims such as “more entropy is better.”

synthesis: The central prediction of Atick–Redlich theory is not one fixed filter but a filter that changes with SNR: high SNR permits strong decorrelation, while low SNR favors spatial averaging and denoising. Approximate translation invariance of natural scenes makes covariance depend only on displacement, allowing Fourier modes to diagonalize convolution and covariance. Natural-image power falls approximately with inverse squared spatial frequency. Perfect whitening would boost high frequencies, but optics, photoreceptors, and noise suppress excessive high-frequency gain.
commonTraps: Treating the Fourier transform as a table of physically meaningless formulas.

Assuming complex numbers introduce an additional biological variable; they are a representational tool.
Using the convolution theorem without a normalization or sign convention.
Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every image.
Letting perfect whitening amplify high frequencies without bound while ignoring optics and noise.
Comparing only firing rates in an adaptation experiment and not the filter or nonlinearity.
Do not teach the Fourier transform as a formula table. Always explain the physical meaning of spatial frequency for an image and receptive field, and state what amplitude and phase each represent.

synthesis: Feedforward cascades can construct selectivity and invariance stage by stage, but descriptive blocks do not automatically identify biological mechanisms. Complex cells are approximately invariant to grating phase, so a single linear STA can be zero; a quadrature-pair square-and-sum energy model is a minimal explanation. Surround suppression likewise is not simply “more inhibition”: recurrent E/I dynamics can make excitation and inhibition fall together, with excitation falling more. Nullclines show the fixed-point shift, while Jacobian stability and an unstable E-only subsystem establish an inhibition-stabilized regime.

synthesis: Motor control consists of closed-loop dynamics among brain, body, and environment, and neural activity is highly distributed. In a linear recurrent network, transforming individual neuronal activities into eigenmode coordinates decouples the system so each mode behaves like an independent first-order process. Eigenvalue \(\lambda\) sets effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\): \(\lambda <1\) decays, \(\lambda \approx 1\) has long memory, \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator, and \(\lambda >1\) grows without bound.
commonTraps: Restricting a motor signal to one region and overlooking distributed population activity.
Confusing neuronal activity coordinates with eigenmode coordinates.
Treating an eigenmode as one neuron.
Writing \(V^{-1}WV=D\) without checking the convention that columns of V are right eigenvectors.
Using \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\) as a positive decay time when \(\lambda >1\).
Assuming \(\lambda =1\) is automatically robust, despite its sensitivity to perturbation.
Analyzing neural dynamics without body and environmental feedback.
Distinguish individual-neuron activity, population-mode coordinates, and behavioral state; do not turn an eigenmode into one “special neuron.”

errata.originalIssue: On page 4, \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}<0\) should be interpreted as exponential growth and an unstable fixed point, not a negative physical time constant.
errata.explanation: For real \(\lambda _{i}<1\), \(\alpha _{i}(t)=\alpha _{i}(0)\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})t/\tau ]\), so the effective time constant is \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\).
